TRANSFORMATIVE USE: THE FIRST AMENDMENT DEFENSE TO A CALIFORNIA RIGHT OF PUBLICITY CLAIM — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This sheet describes the First Amendment defense that California courts apply to a right of publicity claim: the transformative use test announced by the California Supreme Court in Comedy III Productions, Inc. v. Gary Saderup, Inc. (2001) 25 Cal.4th 387 and applied by that court in Winter v. DC Comics (2003) 30 Cal.4th 881, together with the two earlier decisions on which Comedy III built, Zacchini v. Scripps-Howard Broadcasting Co. (1977) 433 U.S. 562 and Guglielmi v. Spelling-Goldberg Productions (1979) 25 Cal.3d 860.

It is a survey of what those opinions say. It sets out the elements of the publicity claim itself only so far as the constitutional decisions describe them; this project's separate information sheets on Civil Code sections 3344 and 3344.1 and on model and publicity releases cover the statutory claim, its exceptions, its remedies, and consent.

This sheet does not evaluate A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015., does not say whether the use of the identity of Taylor Morgan in that work is or is not transformative, and does not predict how any court would rule. It records the authorities and stops there. It is prepared by Jordan Alex Lee as of September 14, 2026 for reference only, and it is not legal advice.

RECORDING THE WORK AND THE IDENTITY AT ISSUE
For reference alongside the authorities set out below, this sheet records the following, as supplied by Jordan Alex Lee.

The work said to be at issue: A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015.

The person whose name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness is said to appear in or on that work: Taylor Morgan.

Date of this reference copy: September 14, 2026.

Nothing in this description is a finding. The cases described below turn on the content of the work as the court views it, and the descriptions recorded here have not been tested against any of those authorities.

THE FEDERAL BASELINE: ZACCHINI AND THE PERFORMER'S ENTIRE ACT
The United States Supreme Court has decided one right of publicity case. In Zacchini v. Scripps-Howard Broadcasting Co. (1977) 433 U.S. 562, a television station filmed a human cannonball act at a county fair and broadcast the whole of it on a news program. The Ohio Supreme Court had held the broadcast privileged; the United States Supreme Court reversed.

The Court described the state interest behind a right of publicity as an interest in the performer's proprietary stake in the act, and distinguished it from the reputational interest that underlies a false light claim. It reasoned that broadcasting the entire act threatened the economic value of the performance, and it held that the First and Fourteenth Amendments do not immunize a broadcaster who airs a performer's entire act without consent.

The Court described its own holding narrowly, and the case concerned the appropriation of a complete performance rather than the use of a name or likeness in an expressive work. Comedy III later cited Zacchini for the proposition that a literal depiction or imitation of a celebrity for commercial gain, adding no significant expression, does not displace the state's interest.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-14]

  — Zacchini v. Scripps-Howard Broadcasting Co., 433 U.S. 562, 573 (1977) (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-433/pdf/USREPORTS-433-562.pdf)
  "Wherever the line in particular situations is to be drawn between media reports that are protected and those that are not, we are quite sure that the First and Fourteenth Amendments do not immunize the media when they broadcast a performer’s entire act without his consent."
  — Zacchini v. Scripps-Howard Broadcasting Co., 433 U.S. 562, 574-575 (1977) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/433/562)
  "The broadcast of a film of petitioner’s entire act poses a substantial threat to the economic value of that performance."
  — Zacchini v. Scripps-Howard Broadcasting Co., 433 U.S. 562, 575 (1977) (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-433/pdf/USREPORTS-433-562.pdf)
  Known gap: Zacchini was fetched from two genuinely independent publishers plus a third: the Government Publishing Office's scan of the bound United States Reports (govinfo, collection USREPORTS, volume 433, granule 433-562), Cornell University's Legal Information Institute, and CourtListener. The govinfo PDF was extracted twice, with pypdf and with pdfminer.six, and the quoted spans are identical in both extractions. One artifact was normalized: the Cornell rendering wraps lines inside the first quoted sentence and uses straight rather than typographic apostrophes, so the match there required collapsing whitespace and folding apostrophe glyphs; the govinfo and CourtListener renderings match the quote exactly as written.

A defect in the official scan is disclosed rather than corrected. In the govinfo bound-volume PDF the majority's own statement of the holding is split across the 574/575 page break by the running head 'ZACCHINI v. SCRIPPS-HOWARD BROADCASTING CO. 575 562 Opinion of the Court', so no contiguous verbatim copy of that sentence exists in the majority opinion as that file extracts. The contiguous copy quoted here appears in the same file in Justice Powell's dissent, which reproduces the sentence in full and pin cites it as 'Ante, at 574-575'; the pin cite given here follows the dissent's own citation. The same govinfo scan carries visible optical-character-recognition damage elsewhere in the case ('cert, denied' for 'cert. denied', 'a, decidedly beneficial effect', 'Pow el l, J., dissenting', 'lastminute'), none of it inside the spans quoted here.

Zacchini construes the First and Fourteenth Amendments, not California's statutes. It does not decide what the California right of publicity covers, and it does not decide any question about a work that is less than a performer's whole act.

GUGLIELMI: A FICTIONALIZED PORTRAYAL, AND THE STATUS OF CHIEF JUSTICE BIRD'S CONCURRENCE
Two years after Zacchini, the California Supreme Court decided Guglielmi v. Spelling-Goldberg Productions (1979) 25 Cal.3d 860, which concerned a television film about Rudolph Valentino presented as a romantic fiction. Chief Justice Bird, concurring, surveyed the decisions that had considered the right of publicity against expressive activity and wrote that, whether the publication was factual and biographical or fictional, the right of publicity had not been held to outweigh the value of free expression. The concurrence added that where the underlying work was protected, it was of no moment that advertising for the film may have increased its profitability.

Comedy III treated that concurrence, and not the Guglielmi majority, as the controlling statement of California law on the point. A footnote in Comedy III explains that the concurrence was signed by two other justices and that its principles were endorsed by a fourth who declined to join the opinion on a separate ground, and states that Chief Justice Bird's views in Guglielmi commanded the support of a majority of the court; Comedy III then says that all its later references to Guglielmi are to the Chief Justice's opinion.

  "it is of no moment that the advertisements may have increased the profitability of the film"

The second Guglielmi quotation, about advertising for the film, and the Comedy III footnote quotation about the concurrence's support, were each found in only one reachable publisher, CourtListener. Every non-CourtListener free publisher of California case law reachable from this environment was tried; Justia, FindLaw, Google Scholar, case.law, Casetext, Leagle, the Internet Archive and vLex are all blocked at the network layer, the California Courts opinion archive returns HTTP 404 for a 2001 docket number, and govinfo full-text searches for both phrases returned zero results. THE STATUTE COMEDY III CONSTRUED WAS FORMER CIVIL CODE SECTION 990, RENUMBERED AS SECTION 3344.1 WHILE REVIEW WAS PENDING
Comedy III arose from charcoal drawings of The Three Stooges, reproduced on lithographs and on T-shirts and sold by the artist. The Three Stooges were deceased personalities, so the claim was brought under the descendible statutory right of publicity enacted in 1984, which at the time of trial and of the appeal was numbered Civil Code section 990.

A footnote in the opinion records that after review was granted the Legislature renumbered that statute as Civil Code section 3344.1, and amended its wording in several respects, and that the court was interpreting the former statute and would refer to it throughout as section 990. The trial court and the Court of Appeal had ruled for the right of publicity holder, and the California Supreme Court affirmed.

The constitutional analysis that follows in the opinion is framed against that statute. The companion statute for living persons, Civil Code section 3344, is described in the opinion as the model on which the 1984 statute was based, and the opinion notes that many key provisions of the two schemes were identical.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-14]

  — Comedy III Productions, Inc. v. Gary Saderup, Inc., 25 Cal.4th 387, fn. 1 (2001) (no page pin cite given; see gap) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2570714/comedy-iii-productions-inc-v-gary-saderup-inc/)
  Known gap: The footnote quoted here was found in only one reachable publisher, CourtListener; a govinfo full-text search for the sentence returned zero results, and no other free publisher of California case law was reachable from this environment. It is quoted without a page pin cite because CourtListener relocates the opinion's footnotes into a block after the disposition and the star markers inside that block no longer track the page on which the footnote text appears.

The CourtListener rendering of Comedy III carries visible optical-character-recognition damage, disclosed here rather than corrected: it prints 'violation of section 990 arid related business torts' for 'and', 'Kennard, I.,' for 'Kennard, J.,' in the concurrence line, and 'subd. (n)(l)' with a lowercase letter l for the numeral 1. None of that damage is inside any span quoted in this sheet.

What the court said about the renumbering is a statement about the statute as it stood before the 1999 amendments. This sheet does not carry forward any holding about the current text of section 3344.1, and it says nothing about whether the transformative use analysis applies in the same terms to a claim under section 3344 for a living person; Comedy III did not decide that question, and no case deciding it was retrieved for this sheet.

COMEDY III'S STARTING PREMISE: THE RIGHT OF PUBLICITY IS AN ECONOMIC RIGHT, NOT A RIGHT OF CENSORSHIP
Before announcing a test, Comedy III set out a premise it said any test must incorporate: that the right of publicity cannot, consistent with the First Amendment, be a right to control a celebrity's image by censoring disagreeable portrayals. Once a person has come forward into the limelight, the opinion states, the First Amendment dictates that the right to comment on, parody, lampoon, and make other expressive uses of the celebrity image must be given broad scope.

From that the court drew what it called the necessary implication: that the right of publicity is essentially an economic right. What the holder possesses, the opinion says, is not a right of censorship but a right to prevent others from misappropriating the economic value generated by the celebrity's fame through the merchandising of the name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness of the celebrity.

That framing governs the rest of the opinion. The question the court then asks is not whether a depiction is flattering or unflattering, but whether the value the defendant captures is the celebrity's or the defendant's own.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-14]
  "not a right of censorship, but a right to prevent others from misappropriating the economic value generated by the celebrity’s fame"
  — Comedy III Productions, Inc. v. Gary Saderup, Inc., 25 Cal.4th 387, 403 (2001) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2570714/comedy-iii-productions-inc-v-gary-saderup-inc/)
  Known gap: The quoted span was fetched from CourtListener and independently confirmed in the Third Circuit's published opinion in Hart v. Electronic Arts, Inc., 717 F.3d 141 (3d Cir. 2013), as published by govinfo (package USCOURTS-ca3-11-03750), which reproduces it and pin cites it as Comedy III, 21 P.3d at 807. Two normalizations were applied to reach the match and are disclosed here: the pypdf extraction of that PDF inserts a space inside the word 'economic', which pdfminer.six does not, so whitespace was collapsed and interior spaces disregarded; and the font in that PDF maps the apostrophe to a double-low-reversed-comma glyph, so apostrophe glyphs were folded before comparison. The CourtListener text matches the quote exactly as written.

Hart is a federal court of appeals opinion applying California law, and it is used here only as an independent publisher's reproduction of the words of a California Supreme Court opinion, not as authority on what California law is.

This clause states a premise, not a rule of decision. Comedy III's premise about censorship does not itself resolve any case, and the opinion says so by immediately asking how courts may distinguish protected from unprotected expression.

WHERE THE TEST CAME FROM: ONE FACTOR OF THE COPYRIGHT FAIR USE ANALYSIS, NOT THE WHOLE OF IT
Comedy III considered and rejected the wholesale importation of the copyright fair use defense into right of publicity law, but took from it the first statutory factor, the purpose and character of the use, and in particular the Campbell v. Acuff-Rose Music, Inc. formulation asking whether and to what extent a new work is transformative. The opinion states that the inquiry into whether a work is transformative is necessarily at the heart of any judicial attempt to square the right of publicity with the First Amendment.

The court gave a reason grounded in the interest the right of publicity protects. Where a work contains significant transformative elements, the opinion says, it is not only especially worthy of First Amendment protection but is also less likely to interfere with the economic interest the right of publicity protects, because parodies and other distortions of a celebrity figure are not good substitutes, from the fan's viewpoint, for conventional depictions.

The borrowing is partial by design. The opinion declines to carry over the fourth fair use factor, the effect of the use on the potential market, on the ground that a separate market inquiry would not usefully supplement the test it was announcing.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-14]

  "when a work contains significant transformative elements, it is not only especially worthy of First Amendment protection, but it is also less likely to interfere with the economic interest protected by the right of publicity"
  — Comedy III Productions, Inc. v. Gary Saderup, Inc., 25 Cal.4th 387, 405 (2001) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2570714/comedy-iii-productions-inc-v-gary-saderup-inc/)
  Known gap: The quotation beginning 'when a work contains significant transformative elements' was fetched from CourtListener and independently confirmed in the Ninth Circuit's en banc-panel opinion in In re NCAA Student-Athlete Name & Likeness Licensing Litigation (Keller), as published by govinfo (package USCOURTS-ca9-10-15387), which reproduces it verbatim and pin cites it as Comedy III, 21 P.3d at 808; that PDF was extracted with pypdf and with pdfminer.six and both extractions contain the span exactly. No normalization was needed.

The sentence about the inquiry being at the heart of the attempt to square the two bodies of law was found in only one reachable publisher, CourtListener. A govinfo full-text search for that sentence returned zero results, and no other free publisher of California case law was reachable from this environment, so for that quotation 'fetched twice' means two fetches of a single publisher.

A scope warning belongs here. The transformative use inquiry described in this sheet is a First Amendment defense to a right of publicity claim. It is not the copyright fair use analysis, and this project's separate copyright fair use information sheet describes that statutory analysis, including the Supreme Court's 2023 treatment of the first fair use factor in Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, Inc. v. Goldsmith. No decision applying Warhol to a California right of publicity claim was retrieved or read for this sheet, and nothing here should be read as saying how the two lines of authority interact.

THE CORE INQUIRY: RAW MATERIAL OR SUM AND SUBSTANCE
Comedy III states the inquiry in two ways. One asks whether the celebrity likeness is one of the raw materials from which an original work is synthesized, or whether the depiction or imitation of the celebrity is the very sum and substance of the work in question. The other asks whether a product containing a celebrity's likeness is so transformed that it has become primarily the defendant's own expression rather than the celebrity's likeness. The opinion adds that by expression it means expression of something other than the likeness of the celebrity.

The opinion is explicit that the transformative elements or creative contributions that earn First Amendment protection are not confined to parody, and that they can take many forms, from factual reporting to fictionalized portrayal and from heavy-handed lampooning to subtle social criticism.

Winter later quoted both formulations as the statement of the test and applied them.

TWO CAUTIONS: ARTISTIC QUALITY IS NOT THE MEASURE, AND SKILL DOES NOT SAVE A LITERAL DEPICTION
Comedy III attached two cautions to the inquiry. The first is that in deciding whether a work is transformative, courts are not to be concerned with the quality of the artistic contribution, because vulgar forms of expression fully qualify for First Amendment protection. The second runs the other way: a literal depiction of a celebrity, even if accomplished with great skill, may still be subject to a right of publicity challenge.

The opinion then characterizes the inquiry as in a sense more quantitative than qualitative, asking whether the literal and imitative elements or the creative elements predominate in the work.

Winter reproduced both cautions and the quantitative-qualitative sentence as part of its summary of the Comedy III test.

THE SUBSIDIARY INQUIRY FOR CLOSE CASES: WHERE THE WORK'S VALUE COMES FROM
Comedy III offers a further question that it says courts may find useful in determining whether a work is sufficiently transformative, particularly in close cases: whether the marketability and economic value of the challenged work derive primarily from the fame of the celebrity depicted.

The opinion states the consequence in one direction only. If that question is answered in the negative, there would generally be no actionable right of publicity, and where the value of the work comes principally from some source other than the celebrity's fame - from the creativity, skill, and reputation of the artist - sufficient transformative elements may be presumed. If the question is answered in the affirmative, the opinion says, it does not follow that the work is without First Amendment protection, because it may still be a transformative work.

Winter restated that asymmetry in the same terms.

HOW THE COURT SUMMARIZED THE RULE: AN AFFIRMATIVE DEFENSE STATED IN THE ALTERNATIVE
Comedy III closes its statement of the test by summarizing it. When an artist is faced with a right of publicity challenge to his or her work, the opinion says, the artist may raise as an affirmative defense that the work is protected by the First Amendment inasmuch as it contains significant transformative elements, or that the value of the work does not derive primarily from the celebrity's fame.

Two features of that sentence are on its face. The defense is described as an affirmative defense, and it is stated in the alternative, so that either branch is offered as sufficient.

Winter quoted this summary as the rule and then applied it.

A related textual point is recorded rather than smoothed over. The Comedy III sentence as CourtListener prints it reads 'he or she may raise as affirmative defense', without the article 'an'. CourtListener's Winter quotes the same sentence with a bracketed insertion, 'may raise as [an] affirmative defense', which is how a later opinion signals that it is supplying a word the original omits. The quotation below begins after that point and so takes no position on the article; the body supplies 'an' in its own prose, not inside the quotation.

HOW COMEDY III CAME OUT: CHARCOAL DRAWINGS OF THE THREE STOOGES
Applying its own test, the Comedy III court examined the drawings and could discern no significant transformative or creative contribution. The artist's skill, the opinion says, was manifestly subordinated to the overall goal of creating literal, conventional depictions of The Three Stooges so as to exploit their fame. Turning to the subsidiary inquiry, the court found that the marketability and economic value of the work derived primarily from the fame of the celebrities depicted, and that it could perceive no transformative elements that would require protection.

The opinion is careful about what that result does not mean. It states that the court does not hold that all reproductions of celebrity portraits are unprotected, and it gives Andy Warhol's silkscreens of celebrity images as an example of work that, through distortion and manipulation of context, may well be entitled to First Amendment protection. It also rejects the trial court's and the Court of Appeal's rationale that reproductions made to be sold for profit are categorically outside the First Amendment, observing that a published book does not receive less protection than the original manuscript because it is one of many copies.

The judgment of the Court of Appeal was affirmed.

WINTER V. DC COMICS: THE SAME TEST, THE OPPOSITE RESULT
Winter v. DC Comics (2003) 30 Cal.4th 881 applied Comedy III to comic books featuring two villainous half-human, half-worm characters named Johnny and Edgar Autumn, drawn with long white hair and pale features, which the musicians Johnny and Edgar Winter said evoked them.

The court reviewed the comic books, attached a representative page to the opinion, and said it could readily ascertain that they were not just conventional depictions of the plaintiffs but contained significant expressive content other than the plaintiffs' mere likenesses. The books did not depict the plaintiffs literally; the plaintiffs were merely part of the raw materials from which the comic books were synthesized; to the extent the drawings resembled them at all, they were distorted for purposes of lampoon, parody, or caricature; and the characters were cartoon figures in a larger story that was itself quite expressive.

The court added that the portrayals did not greatly threaten the plaintiffs' right of publicity, because fans who wanted pictures of the Winters would find the drawings of the Autumn brothers unsatisfactory as a substitute for conventional depictions. It concluded that the comic books were transformative and entitled to First Amendment protection, and that the Court of Appeal had erred in finding triable issues of fact.

THREE THINGS WINTER SAID DO NOT MATTER: LITERARY CATEGORY, MARKETING, AND THE NEED FOR A TRIAL
Winter addressed and rejected three arguments about how the test should be run.

First, literary category. The plaintiffs argued that the comic books did not technically qualify as a parody of them. The court answered that the distinction between parody and other forms of literary expression is irrelevant to the Comedy III transformative test, that it does not matter what precise literary category the work falls into, and that what matters is whether the work is transformative, not whether it is parody or satire or caricature or serious social commentary or any other specific form of expression.

Second, marketing. The plaintiffs pointed to evidence that the defendants had traded on their likenesses and reputations to generate interest in the series. The court called that irrelevant to whether the comic books were constitutionally protected, stating that the question is whether the work is transformative, not how it is marketed, and citing Guglielmi for the proposition that where the work itself is protected, advertising that increases its profitability is of no moment.

Third, the need for a trial. Noting that protracted litigation would chill the exercise of First Amendment rights, the court stated that, as in Comedy III, courts can often resolve the question as a matter of law simply by viewing the work in question and, if necessary, comparing it to an actual likeness of the person portrayed.

The United States Supreme Court has decided one right of publicity case. In Zacchini v. Scripps-Howard Broadcasting Co. (1977) 433 U.S. 562, a television station filmed a human cannonball act at a county fair and broadcast the whole of it on a news program. The Court described the state interest behind a right of publicity as an interest in the performer's proprietary stake in the act, and distinguished it from the reputational interest that underlies a false light claim. It reasoned that broadcasting the entire act threatened the economic value of the performance, and it held that the First and Fourteenth Amendments do not immunize a broadcaster who airs a performer's entire act without consent.

The Court described its own holding narrowly, and the case concerned the appropriation of a complete performance rather than the use of a name or likeness in an expressive work. Comedy III later cited Zacchini for the proposition that a literal depiction or imitation of a celebrity for commercial gain, adding no significant expression, does not displace the state's interest.

Before announcing a test, Comedy III set out a premise it said any test must incorporate: that the right of publicity cannot, consistent with the First Amendment, be a right to control a celebrity's image by censoring disagreeable portrayals. Once a person has come forward into the limelight, the opinion states, the First Amendment dictates that the right to comment on, parody, lampoon, and make other expressive uses of the celebrity image must be given broad scope.

From that the court drew what it called the necessary implication: that the right of publicity is essentially an economic right. What the holder possesses, the opinion says, is not a right of censorship but a right to prevent others from misappropriating the economic value generated by the celebrity's fame through the merchandising of the name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness of the celebrity.

That framing governs the rest of the opinion. The question the court then asks is not whether a depiction is flattering or unflattering, but whether the value the defendant captures is the celebrity's or the defendant's own.

Applying its own test, the Comedy III court examined the drawings and could discern no significant transformative or creative contribution. The artist's skill, the opinion says, was manifestly subordinated to the overall goal of creating literal, conventional depictions of The Three Stooges so as to exploit their fame. Turning to the subsidiary inquiry, the court found that the marketability and economic value of the work derived primarily from the fame of the celebrities depicted, and that it could perceive no transformative elements that would require protection.

The opinion is careful about what that result does not mean. It states that the court does not hold that all reproductions of celebrity portraits are unprotected, and it gives Andy Warhol's silkscreens of celebrity images as an example of work that, through distortion and manipulation of context, may well be entitled to First Amendment protection. It also rejects the trial court's and the Court of Appeal's rationale that reproductions made to be sold for profit are categorically outside the First Amendment, observing that a published book does not receive less protection than the original manuscript because it is one of many copies.

The judgment of the Court of Appeal was affirmed.

Winter v. DC Comics (2003) 30 Cal.4th 881 applied Comedy III to comic books featuring two villainous half-human, half-worm characters named Johnny and Edgar Autumn, drawn with long white hair and pale features, which the musicians Johnny and Edgar Winter said evoked them.

The court reviewed the comic books, attached a representative page to the opinion, and said it could readily ascertain that they were not just conventional depictions of the plaintiffs but contained significant expressive content other than the plaintiffs' mere likenesses. The books did not depict the plaintiffs literally; the plaintiffs were merely part of the raw materials from which the comic books were synthesized; to the extent the drawings resembled them at all, they were distorted for purposes of lampoon, parody, or caricature; and the characters were cartoon figures in a larger story that was itself quite expressive.

The court added that the portrayals did not greatly threaten the plaintiffs' right of publicity, because fans who wanted pictures of the Winters would find the drawings of the Autumn brothers unsatisfactory as a substitute for conventional depictions. It concluded that the comic books were transformative and entitled to First Amendment protection, and that the Court of Appeal had erred in finding triable issues of fact.

expectedJSON.body:
Winter addressed and rejected three arguments about how the test should be run.

First, literary category. The plaintiffs argued that the comic books did not technically qualify as a parody of them. The court answered that the distinction between parody and other forms of literary expression is irrelevant to the Comedy III transformative test, that it does not matter what precise literary category the work falls into, and that what matters is whether the work is transformative, not whether it is parody or satire or caricature or serious social commentary or any other specific form of expression.

Second, marketing. The plaintiffs pointed to evidence that the defendants had traded on their likenesses and reputations to generate interest in the series. The court called that irrelevant to whether the comic books were constitutionally protected, stating that the question is whether the work is transformative, not how it is marketed, and citing Guglielmi for the proposition that where the work itself is protected, advertising that increases its profitability is of no moment.

Third, the need for a trial. Noting that protracted litigation would chill the exercise of First Amendment rights, the court stated that, as in Comedy III, courts can often resolve the question as a matter of law simply by viewing the work in question and, if necessary, comparing it to an actual likeness of the person portrayed.
